results.title: What is the difference between primary and secondary endpoints?
results.content: # What is the difference between primary and secondary endpoints? Understanding the distinction between primary and secondary endpoints is essential for interpreting clinical trial results and their implications for clinical practice. The primary endpoint is the main result that is measured at the end of a study to see if a given treatment has worked. In the context of the same cancer trial, secondary endpoints might include progression-free survival, which measures the time during and after treatment that the patient lives with the disease without it getting worse. Evaluating secondary endpoints can also help to uncover unexpected results that could be clinically significant. While secondary endpoints are valuable, there is a risk of overemphasizing them, especially if the primary endpoint does not show statistically significant results. They rely heavily on the results of primary endpoints while considering secondary endpoints as supplementary data. In clinical research, primary and secondary endpoints complement each other, providing a complete picture of an intervention's efficacy and safety.

results.title: Primary versus secondary endpoints – Primary Care Notebook
results.content: * composite primary endpoints are frequently used to overcome the difficulties associated with designing a study around a single event of interest (e.g. death). * an example of a composite primary endpoint in a cardiovascular study might be cardiovascular death and/or non-fatal myocardial infarction and/or any kind of stroke - thus the study would be designed with such a composite primary endpoint (e.g. any major cardiovascular event) and would require fewer subjects, as the total number of events to be detected is in effect increased. - because the design of the study was not based around the secondary endpoint (s), analyses of secondary endpoints need to be viewed with caution. - the caution in interpreting results is also true with respect to sub-group analyses, in which primary or secondary endpoints are considered in a smaller sub-group of the whole study population (e.g. only those subjects with a specific baseline characteristic) - this is because the power of the study is based on the entire study population.

results.title: A proposed statistical framework for the management of subgroup analyses for large clinical trials - ScienceDirect
results.content: # A proposed statistical framework for the management of subgroup analyses for large clinical trials. Planned and unplanned subgroup analyses of large clinical trials are frequently performed and the results are sometimes difficult to interpret. In this article we provide a general framework to manage subgroup analyses and to interpret the findings through a set of supplement analyses to planned main (primary and secondary) analyses, as an alternative to the commonly used multiple comparison framework. The proposed approach collectively and coherently utilizes several quantitative methods and enhances the credibility and interpretability of subgroup analyses. In addition to the overall primary analysis of a clinical trial, researchers often perform subgroup analyses to evaluate the consistency of the primary finding among various patient subgroups, and to identify whether any subgroup may be more responsive to the study medicine. Statistical methods of multiple comparisons have been used to assess the credibility of subgroup findings, e.g., Luo et al. As a special case, many authors consider the design and interpretation of regional analyses from multi-regional clinical trials [13], [14]. While being helpful to address concerns for a few regions, those investigators reiterate the limitation of any single procedure for assessing many possible subgroup analyses associated with a large clinical trial. The main purpose of this paper is to propose a statistical framework to manage potential subgroup analyses and to interpret their findings. The framework includes four steps: the design consideration; the identification of predictive factors for the study regimen, the evaluation of quantitative and qualitative interactions between treatment and subgroup; and the exploration of extrinsic factors. These steps address multiple possible variations of the study outcome and the ad hoc nature of subgroup analyses. As mentioned in the Introduction section, we propose a four-step framework to manage and evaluate subgroup analyses. As in many real cases, the study did not go through all steps outlined in the complete framework above, however both the data collection and analyses can help provide insights for managing subgroup analyses. In this paper, we reviewed and assembled quantitative methods to form a statistical framework to manage potential subgroup analyses of large clinical trials.

Choose Language Hide Translation Bar. Introducing the Subgroup role in the Response Screening and Fit Model platforms of JMP Pro 19. In **JMP Pro 19** and **JMP Clinical 19**, the new **Subgroup** role makes it easier than ever before to explore endpoints within subgroups of observations. Often, subgroups are selected due to their similarity across one or more characteristics that they share, and there may be interest in performing analyses within these subgroups to understand how results may vary from the analysis of the full set of observations. Throughout this blog post, we illustrate the **Subgroup** role using the **Nicardipine data** available within JMP’s Sample Data Index. Suppose we wanted to compared Patient Death (Y/N) (using the Patient Died Flag, setting the Target Level to Y) between Nicardipine and Placebo (Description of Planned Arm, setting Placebo as the Control arm) within subgroups based on the following factors:. Response Screening analysis with Subgroup role. Response Screening of death within subgroups. With **Subgroup Twoway** selected, these 17 factors produce 612 different subgroups (easily visible from the **Pvalues** data table as there are 612 rows, Save Tables > Save PValues). When a single factor is used to produce a subgroup, as in the first row of the table of Figure 2, **Subgroup2** = All. When two factors are used, both **Subgroup** and **Subgroup2** have non-All values listed. The analysis result in the entire population of patients (here, 882) has **Subgroup** and **Subgroup2** both equal to All. Accounting for all of the multiple tests performed with FDR adjustment, there are no differences observed in the rates of death between the treatment arms. The **Response Screening** personality in **Fit Model** makes it possible to fit more complex models for continuous endpoints to allow for the inclusion of multiple covariates into the analysis of subgroups. **Response Screening** in **JMP Pro 19** and **JMP Clinical 19** makes it easier than ever before to explore results within subgroups. Soon, we’ll discuss the **Subgroup Screening** report within **JMP Clinical** that uses the power of **Response Screening** to gain insight into the primary and key secondary endpoints of clinical trials.
